subject: DBMS
summary: DBMS is the study of how a database keeps your data correct, fast, and alive through crashes - and it is the subject interviewers use to separate people who can write a query from people who know what the query costs. Every question here maps to a production incident you will eventually meet: a slow endpoint (indexing, EXPLAIN), a double-charged customer (transactions, isolation), a dead server that must come back with no lost orders (WAL, recovery). This file teaches the whole chain on ONE running example - a food-delivery app's schema - so keys, normalization, indexes, and transactions all touch the same tables and stay concrete. Study it in order: the storage story (sections 1-5) explains what a query costs, the concurrency story (sections 6-9) explains what runs at the same time, and the last three sections cover the operational questions (EXPLAIN, recovery, CAP) that senior interviewers use to check depth. Do the flashcards daily; rehearse the interview answers out loud.

sections.title: 1. The Relational Model and Keys
sections.content:
Start with the problem the relational model solved. Before it (1970), every application stored data in its own file formats, and programs navigated records by following physical pointers. Change the file layout and every program broke. The relational model's move: store everything as relations (tables) of tuples (rows) with attributes (columns), and let the user say WHAT rows they want while the database decides HOW to fetch them. That separation - logical model vs physical storage - is why you can add an index later and no application code changes. When an interviewer asks "why relational?", they are testing whether you see that separation, not whether you can recite Codd.

This file uses one schema throughout, a food-delivery app:

```
-- The running example for this whole file: a food-delivery app.
customers   (customer_id PK, name, email UNIQUE, city)
restaurants (restaurant_id PK, name, city)
menu_items  (item_id PK, restaurant_id FK, name, price)
orders      (order_id PK, customer_id FK, restaurant_id FK, placed_at, status)
order_items (order_id FK, item_id FK, qty, price_at_order,
             PRIMARY KEY (order_id, item_id))
```

Now keys, which exist because rows need identity. A superkey is any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row - in customers, {customer_id, email, name} works, but it carries dead weight. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: remove any column and it stops being unique. customers has two candidate keys: {customer_id} and {email}. The primary key is the one candidate key you elect for row identity; the losers become alternate keys and usually get a UNIQUE constraint (email here). Pick the PK for stability and size, not meaning: emails change and are 30+ bytes; an integer id never changes and is 4-8 bytes - and every secondary index in InnoDB stores a copy of the PK, so a fat PK bloats every index (section 5).

A foreign key is a column that stores another table's primary key and asks the database to enforce it: orders.customer_id must exist in customers, or the INSERT fails. That check is referential integrity - orders can never point at a deleted customer. ON DELETE decides the reaction: RESTRICT blocks the delete, CASCADE deletes the orders too, SET NULL orphans them explicitly.

order_items shows a composite key: neither order_id nor item_id alone is unique (one order has many items; one item appears in many orders), but the pair (order_id, item_id) is - so the pair is the primary key, and each half is separately a foreign key.

Interview trap: "primary key vs unique key." A strong answer: a table can have many unique constraints but exactly one PK; PK columns are implicitly NOT NULL while unique columns may hold NULLs (and in most engines several NULLs pass unique); and in InnoDB the PK physically orders the table while a unique index is a separate structure. The interviewer is testing whether you know keys have physical consequences, not only logical ones.

sections.title: 2. ER Modelling: From Boxes to Tables
sections.content:
Why ER modelling exists: CREATE TABLE forces hundreds of small decisions (which table owns the foreign key? do I need a third table?), and getting them wrong is expensive after data exists. An ER (entity-relationship) diagram is the cheap sketch you argue about first. An entity is a thing with identity (Customer, Restaurant, Order); an attribute is a fact about it (city, price); a relationship connects entities and carries a cardinality - 1:1, 1:N, or M:N - which is the single most important thing to read off the diagram, because cardinality decides the table shape.

```
CUSTOMER 1 ----places----< N ORDER N >----from---- 1 RESTAURANT
                              |
                              | M : N  (an order contains many items,
                              v         an item appears in many orders)
                          MENU_ITEM N >---offered by--- 1 RESTAURANT
```

The mapping rules, each shown on the running schema:

1:N - the foreign key goes on the N side. A customer places many orders, so orders carries customer_id. Never the reverse: customers cannot hold "order_ids" because a column stores one value, not a list.

M:N - no foreign key placement works, so you create a junction table (a table whose composite primary key is the two foreign keys). Order-contains-item is M:N, hence order_items(order_id, item_id). Attributes that belong to the RELATIONSHIP, not to either entity, live here: qty and price_at_order describe "this item in this order", so they sit in order_items. When an interviewer asks "where does quantity go?", they are testing exactly this: relationship attributes go on the junction table.

1:1 - a foreign key with a UNIQUE constraint on it, placed on the optional side. If every order has at most one payment record, payments carries order_id UNIQUE, because a payment cannot exist without an order but an unpaid order can exist.

Multivalued attribute - a customer with several phone numbers gets a child table customer_phones(customer_id FK, phone), because one column holds one value (this is also the 1NF rule, section 3).

Weak entity - an entity that has no identity of its own. If menu items were numbered per restaurant ("item 4 at TandooriHub"), menu_items would need PRIMARY KEY (restaurant_id, item_number): the owner's key becomes part of the child's key. We sidestepped that by giving item_id a global id - the common practical choice, because surrogate ids keep foreign keys short.

The habit to demonstrate in interviews: say the cardinality OUT LOUD before proposing tables ("a customer has many orders, an order has one customer, so..."). It shows a method instead of a memorized schema.

sections.title: 3. Normalization: 1NF to BCNF on One Table
sections.content:
Normalization exists because duplicated facts drift apart. Imagine the delivery app kept one spreadsheet-style table:

```
orders_flat
order_id | cust  | cust_city | items_text        | restaurant  | rest_city
101      | Asha  | Pune      | "2x Roll, 1x Coke"| TandooriHub | Pune
102      | Asha  | Pune      | "1x Biryani"      | BiryaniBay  | Pune
103      | Ravi  | Delhi     | "3x Roll"         | TandooriHub | Pune
```

Three concrete failures. Update anomaly: Asha moves to Mumbai - you must edit every row she appears in; miss one and the database now claims two cities. Insert anomaly: a new restaurant with zero orders cannot be recorded at all. Delete anomaly: delete order 102 and BiryaniBay vanishes from existence. Normalization removes these by making every fact live in exactly one place. Each normal form kills one kind of redundancy - the mnemonic is "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."

1NF (atomic values): no lists inside a cell, no repeating groups. "2x Roll, 1x Coke" becomes one row per item with columns (order_id, item_id, item_name, qty, item_price, ...customer and restaurant columns repeated). Now SQL can filter and join on items - you cannot WHERE on the middle of a string.

2NF (the whole key): applies when the key is composite. After 1NF the key is (order_id, item_id). But item_name depends on item_id alone, and cust_city depends on order_id alone - partial dependencies. Every row of order 101 repeats Asha's city; every order of Roll repeats its name. Split them out: menu_items(item_id, name, price) and an orders table keyed by order_id. What remains keyed by (order_id, item_id) is exactly our order_items.

3NF (nothing but the key): kill transitive dependencies - non-key columns determined by other non-key columns. In orders, order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines cust_city, so cust_city rides along transitively. Move customer facts to customers(customer_id, name, email, city). Same for restaurant facts. Result: precisely the running schema of section 1.

BCNF (every determinant is a key): a stricter 3NF for a corner case. Suppose courier scheduling: shifts(courier_id, hour, zone), where a courier works exactly one zone (courier_id determines zone) and each zone has one courier per hour ({zone, hour} determines courier_id). Candidate keys: {courier_id, hour} and {zone, hour}. The dependency courier_id -> zone has a determinant that is not a key - 3NF tolerates it (zone is part of a candidate key), BCNF does not. Decompose: courier_zone(courier_id PK, zone) and courier_hours(courier_id, hour). Interviewers who push to BCNF are testing whether you can spot a dependency, not whether you memorized definitions - practice reading "X determines Y" off a description.

When to denormalize: after you MEASURE that a hot read path is too slow and the join or aggregate is the cost. Example: order total. Normalized, it is SUM(qty * price_at_order) over order_items; if the orders list screen does that for 50 orders per page load, you may add orders.total_amount maintained at write time. The price: every write path must keep the copy in sync, and a bug produces a total that disagrees with its items. So denormalize when reads are frequent, writes are rare, and staleness is detectable - and note that price_at_order itself is NOT denormalization: menu price changes, historical order price must not, so they are different facts.

sections.title: 4. SQL Logical Execution Order
sections.content:
Why this matters: half of everyday SQL confusion ("why can't WHERE see my alias?", "why does HAVING exist?") disappears once you know the order in which the clauses logically apply - which is NOT the order you write them. Take a real query on the running schema: "cities with at least 10 delivered orders, biggest first."

```sql
SELECT   c.city, COUNT(*) AS orders_cnt        -- written 1st, runs 5th
FROM     orders o                              -- runs 1st
JOIN     customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id   -- 2nd
WHERE    o.status = 'delivered'                -- 3rd
GROUP BY c.city                                -- 4th
HAVING   COUNT(*) >= 10                        -- runs after grouping
ORDER BY orders_cnt DESC                       -- 6th (aliases visible now)
LIMIT    5;                                    -- 7th
```

```
FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT
  rows   ->  fewer  ->  groups  -> fewer  -> columns             -> sorted  -> top n
             rows                  groups
```

Consequences you can now derive instead of memorize. (1) WHERE cannot use the alias orders_cnt because SELECT has not run yet when WHERE filters; ORDER BY can, because it runs after SELECT. (2) WHERE vs HAVING is row filter vs group filter: WHERE discards rows BEFORE grouping (cheap - fewer rows to group), HAVING discards whole groups AFTER aggregation (necessary when the condition is an aggregate, like COUNT(*) >= 10). Putting a plain row condition into HAVING gives the same answer but groups garbage first. (3) LIMIT 5 does not save the sort: ORDER BY must determine the top rows before LIMIT cuts (engines optimize this into a top-N heap, but logically sort precedes limit).

One more trap interviewers love - ON vs WHERE with LEFT JOIN. "All customers and their delivered orders, including customers with none":

```sql
-- correct: condition in ON keeps unmatched customers with NULL order columns
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered';

-- wrong: WHERE o.status = 'delivered' runs AFTER the join, and NULL status
-- fails the test - customers with no orders vanish; the LEFT JOIN silently
-- became an INNER JOIN.
```

Last nuance for strong candidates: this order is LOGICAL. The optimizer physically reorders anything it wants (filter pushdown, join reordering) as long as the result set matches what the logical order defines. When the interviewer asks about execution order, they are testing whether you can predict a query's RESULT; when they ask about EXPLAIN (section 10), they are testing whether you can predict its COST.
sections.code:
# The SQL logical pipeline, executed by hand on tiny data - proves the clause order.
orders = [
    {"order_id": 1, "customer_id": 1, "status": "delivered"},
    {"order_id": 2, "customer_id": 1, "status": "delivered"},
    {"order_id": 3, "customer_id": 2, "status": "cancelled"},
    {"order_id": 4, "customer_id": 3, "status": "delivered"},
]
customers = [
    {"customer_id": 1, "city": "Pune"},
    {"customer_id": 2, "city": "Pune"},
    {"customer_id": 3, "city": "Delhi"},
]

# FROM + JOIN
joined = [{**o, **c} for o in orders for c in customers
          if o["customer_id"] == c["customer_id"]]
# WHERE (before grouping - aliases do not exist yet)
filtered = [r for r in joined if r["status"] == "delivered"]
# GROUP BY city
groups = {}
for r in filtered:
    groups.setdefault(r["city"], []).append(r)
# HAVING (filters whole groups, may use aggregates)
kept = {city: rows for city, rows in groups.items() if len(rows) >= 2}
# SELECT (aliases born here) -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT
result = sorted([{"city": c, "orders_cnt": len(rs)} for c, rs in kept.items()],
                key=lambda r: -r["orders_cnt"])[:5]

assert result == [{"city": "Pune", "orders_cnt": 2}]
# Delhi had 1 delivered order: the group existed, HAVING removed it.
assert "Delhi" in groups and "Delhi" not in kept
print("logical order verified:", result)

sections.title: 5. Indexing: B+ Trees, Clustered vs Secondary, Covering
sections.content:
The problem first. orders has 10 million rows; "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42" without an index reads all 10M rows - a sequential scan, seconds of I/O for maybe 30 matching rows. An index is a separate, sorted structure that lets the engine jump to those 30 rows. Nearly every relational engine uses a B+ tree: a balanced tree where internal nodes hold only separator keys for routing, ALL actual entries live in the leaves, and the leaves are linked left-to-right so range scans walk a linked list instead of re-descending.

```
                     [ 40 |  80 ]              internal: routing only
                    /      |     \
            [10|25]     [55|70]     [90|95]
            /  |  \       ...         ...
leaves: [3,7]->[10,17]->[25,31]->[41,55]->...->[95,99]
         ^ sorted, linked ->  range scan = walk right
```

Why B+ and not alternatives - the numbers make the case. Nodes are disk pages (16KB in InnoDB, 8KB in Postgres), so fanout is in the hundreds: with fanout 300, a 3-level tree indexes 300^3 = 27 million keys and any lookup costs 3 page reads, of which the top levels are almost always cached - so a point lookup on 27M rows touches disk maybe once. A binary search tree with fanout 2 would be ~25 levels = 25 reads. A hash index gives O(1) exact lookups but NO ranges ("placed_at > yesterday") and no sorted order for ORDER BY - which is why B+ trees are the default and hash indexes are a niche.

Clustered vs secondary - the question interviewers use to check real understanding. A clustered index IS the table: in InnoDB the whole row lives in the leaf of the primary key's B+ tree, so the table is physically ordered by PK and a PK lookup lands directly on the row. A secondary index (any other index) stores in its leaves only the indexed column plus the primary key value. So "find orders by customer_id" via a secondary index is TWO tree descents: secondary tree -> get PK -> PK tree -> get row. This is also why a fat PK hurts: it is copied into every secondary leaf. Postgres differs: tables are heaps (unordered row files), every index is secondary, and leaves hold a TID (physical row address) instead of the PK - one descent plus one heap fetch.

Covering index: if the index itself contains every column the query needs, the second lookup vanishes - an index-only scan. Index (customer_id, placed_at) covers "SELECT placed_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY placed_at": equality on the first column, presorted on the second, no table visit at all. Column ORDER inside a composite index matters: (customer_id, placed_at) serves that query; (placed_at, customer_id) does not, because the tree is sorted by placed_at first and customer 42's entries are scattered.

When indexes hurt - always give this unprompted. (1) Writes: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update every index; 5 secondary indexes turn one row write into 6 B+ tree modifications. (2) Low selectivity: an index on status with 3 values matching ~33% of rows is useless - reading a third of the table through random index hops is slower than one sequential scan, and the optimizer will rightly ignore it. (3) Functions kill index use: WHERE lower(email) = '...' cannot use a plain index on email (the tree is sorted by email, not lower(email)) - fix with an expression index or by storing normalized data. (4) Tiny tables: a 50-row table fits in one page; a scan beats a descent.
sections.code:
# B+ tree arithmetic + a working search over a 2-level tree.
import math

fanout, rows = 300, 10_000_000
height = math.ceil(math.log(rows, fanout))     # levels of descent
assert height == 3          # 300^3 = 27M >= 10M rows -> 3 page reads per lookup
assert math.log2(rows) > 23 # a binary tree would need 20+ levels instead

# Tiny B+ tree: root routes by separator keys; leaves hold entries and link right.
leaves = [[3, 7], [10, 17], [25, 31], [41, 55]]   # sorted, "linked" by list order
seps   = [10, 25, 41]        # child i holds keys < seps[i]; last child holds the rest

def search(key):
    i = 0
    while i < len(seps) and key >= seps[i]:
        i += 1                                   # descend: pick child by separator
    return i, key in leaves[i]

def range_scan(lo, hi):
    i, _ = search(lo)                            # one descent to the start leaf...
    out = []
    while i < len(leaves):                       # ...then walk the leaf chain
        out += [k for k in leaves[i] if lo <= k <= hi]
        if leaves[i] and leaves[i][-1] > hi:
            break
        i += 1
    return out

assert search(17) == (1, True) and search(18) == (1, False)
assert range_scan(9, 30) == [10, 17, 25]         # crosses leaves without re-descending
print("height for 10M rows @ fanout 300:", height, "page reads")

sections.title: 6. Transactions and ACID (One Bank Transfer)
sections.content:
The problem: real operations span several writes, and the world can fail between them. The canonical example - transfer 500 from account A (balance 2000) to account B (balance 100):

```
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 'A';   -- step 1
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 'B';   -- step 2
COMMIT;

crash after step 1, before step 2:
  A = 1500, B = 100  -> 500 rupees ceased to exist.
```

A transaction is the database's promise that a group of statements behaves as one unit, and ACID names the four parts of the promise. Walk each letter through the transfer - this is the exact structure of a strong interview answer.

Atomicity - all or nothing. If the crash happens after step 1, recovery must roll the debit back so the outcome is "transfer never happened" (A=2000, B=100), never the half state. Mechanism: the engine keeps undo information (InnoDB's undo log, Postgres's old row versions), so an aborted or interrupted transaction's writes can be reversed. Atomicity is about FAILURE, not about concurrency.

Consistency - the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid state. Two layers: constraints the database enforces (balance >= 0 as a CHECK, foreign keys), and invariants the application owns (the SUM of both balances is unchanged by a transfer - no constraint can say that; your transaction's logic must). If step 1 would drive A negative, the statement fails and atomicity cancels the rest. Saying "C is partly the app's job" marks you as someone who has thought about it.

Isolation - concurrent transactions must not see each other's half-done work. While the transfer sits between step 1 and step 2, an auditor running SELECT SUM(balance) must not see 1500 + 100 = 1600 (money missing!). It must see either the before-state sum 2100 or the after-state sum 2100 - "as if the transactions ran one after another." How strictly this holds is tunable (isolation levels, section 8), because perfect isolation costs concurrency.

Durability - once COMMIT returns to your code, the transfer survives a power cut. Mechanism: before COMMIT returns, the change records are fsynced to the write-ahead log on disk (section 11); the data pages themselves can follow later, because the log can replay them. Durability is a promise about the moment COMMIT RETURNS - a crash one microsecond later loses nothing.

Interview framing: when asked "explain ACID," weak candidates recite four words; strong candidates run one example through all four letters and name the mechanism behind each (undo log, constraints+app invariants, isolation levels, WAL). That mapping - letter to mechanism - is what is actually being tested.

sections.title: 7. Concurrency Problems: Three Interleavings to Memorize
sections.content:
Why these exist: databases interleave transactions for throughput - hundreds of them in flight, their reads and writes shuffled together. Interleaving is safe until two transactions touch the same data; then specific, named anomalies appear. Interviewers ask for these BY INTERLEAVING - "show me the schedule" - because anyone can recite definitions. Learn one concrete timeline for each. (Time flows downward; T1 and T2 are concurrent transactions.)

Dirty read - reading data that was never committed:

```
T1: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal=1500 WHERE id='A';
T2:                          BEGIN; SELECT bal WHERE id='A';  -- sees 1500 (uncommitted!)
T2:                          -- approves a loan based on 1500
T1: ROLLBACK;                -- A is 2000 again; "1500" never existed
```

T2 made a decision on a value that, after the rollback, never existed in any committed state. This is why READ UNCOMMITTED is essentially never used.

Non-repeatable read - the same ROW gives two different answers inside one transaction:

```
T2: BEGIN; SELECT bal WHERE id='A';         -- 2000
T1:        BEGIN; UPDATE ... bal=1500 WHERE id='A'; COMMIT;
T2:        SELECT bal WHERE id='A';         -- 1500. Same query, same txn, new answer.
```

Deadly when T2 read the value to validate, then reads again to act - the ground moved between.

Phantom read - the same PREDICATE returns new rows (no existing row changed; rows APPEARED):

```
T2: BEGIN; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE city='Pune';   -- 10
T1:        INSERT INTO orders (..., city='Pune'); COMMIT;
T2:        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE city='Pune';   -- 11: a phantom
```

The distinction from non-repeatable: locking the rows T2 read cannot prevent phantoms, because the problem row did not exist yet - preventing it needs predicate/gap locking or snapshots (section 9).

Bonus anomaly that costs real money - the lost update, a race condition (two transactions doing read-modify-write on the same row, where one write overwrites the other): both read bal=100, both compute 100+10, both write 110 - one deposit vanished. Fixes, in order of preference: make the write atomic (UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 10 - the read and write become one locked statement); or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to lock the row through the read; or optimistic locking with a version column (UPDATE ... WHERE id=1 AND version=7 - zero rows updated means someone beat you; retry). Naming the lost update unprompted, with its fix, is a reliable way to stand out.

sections.title: 8. Isolation Levels: Mapping Levels to Anomalies
sections.content:
Perfect isolation (every transaction behaves as if it ran alone) is expensive - it forces waiting or aborting. So SQL defines four levels that trade anomalies for speed, and the whole topic is one table. Reproduce it on the whiteboard the moment isolation comes up:

```
level             | dirty read | non-repeatable | phantom
------------------+------------+----------------+------------
READ UNCOMMITTED  | possible   | possible       | possible
READ COMMITTED    | no         | possible       | possible
REPEATABLE READ   | no         | no             | possible*
SERIALIZABLE      | no         | no             | no
                                 (* see engine notes below)
```

How each level achieves its row, in terms of section 7's interleavings. READ COMMITTED: every statement sees only committed data as of the moment THAT STATEMENT starts - kills dirty reads, but two statements in one transaction get two snapshots, so non-repeatable reads and phantoms remain. REPEATABLE READ: the whole transaction reads from one snapshot taken at its first read - the same row always answers the same, and in snapshot implementations the same predicate does too. SERIALIZABLE: the result must equal SOME serial (one-after-another) ordering of the transactions; anything that cannot be serialized blocks or aborts.

Now the engine reality, because interviewers at good companies push past the standard. Postgres: default is READ COMMITTED; READ UNCOMMITTED exists as a name but behaves as READ COMMITTED (MVCC never shows uncommitted data, so there is nothing dirty to read). Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation - phantoms cannot appear (the snapshot is fixed), but a subtler anomaly called write skew can: two transactions each read both on-call doctors, each removes a DIFFERENT one, both commit, zero doctors remain - each decision was valid against its snapshot, the combination broke the invariant. Postgres SERIALIZABLE (SSI) detects such dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction with a serialization error - your code must retry. InnoDB/MySQL: default is REPEATABLE READ; consistent reads use a snapshot, and locking reads (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) additionally take next-key locks (row lock + lock on the gap before it) that block other transactions from inserting phantoms into scanned ranges.

Choosing, with the criteria stated: stay on the default (RC in Postgres) and make read-modify-write paths explicit with atomic UPDATEs or FOR UPDATE when the anomaly you fear is the lost update; use REPEATABLE READ when a multi-statement report must be internally consistent (all statements one snapshot); use SERIALIZABLE when an invariant spans multiple rows (the doctors case) AND you can wrap transactions in retry loops. When the interviewer asks "which level would you pick," they are testing whether you choose by NAMED ANOMALY - the answer "RC, plus FOR UPDATE where I read-then-write, because what I actually fear is the lost update" beats "serializable to be safe."

sections.title: 9. Locking vs MVCC: How Postgres and InnoDB Really Isolate
sections.content:
Isolation levels are a spec; this section is the two mechanisms that implement them. The old way is pure locking: a shared lock (S - many readers may hold it) to read, an exclusive lock (X - one holder, excludes everything) to write, held until commit under two-phase locking (acquire locks as you go, release nothing until the end - this discipline is what makes schedules serializable). Correct, but readers block writers and writers block readers - a 10-second report SELECT stalls every UPDATE it overlaps. And lock waiting brings deadlock: T1 locks row A and wants B, T2 locks B and wants A - a cycle where each waits forever. Engines detect the cycle (or time out) and kill one transaction as the victim; the fix on your side is to retry the victim, and to prevent recurrence, lock rows in a consistent order (always lower account id first).

MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) is the modern answer: instead of blocking readers, keep multiple versions of each row, and give every transaction a consistent snapshot - readers never block writers, writers never block readers. Writers still take row-level X locks against EACH OTHER (two UPDATEs to one row queue up), but reads glide past everything.

The two implementations - naming these specifics is what "senior" sounds like:

```
Postgres: versions live IN the table (heap)
  update bal 2000 -> 1500 by txn 900:
  [xmin=612, xmax=900 | A | 2000]   old version, now dead to txns after 900
  [xmin=900, xmax= -  | A | 1500]   new version, appended to the heap
  visibility: a txn sees a version if xmin committed before its snapshot
              and xmax (deleter) had not. Dead versions pile up -> VACUUM
              reclaims them (autovacuum); skipping it means table bloat.

InnoDB: ONE current version in the clustered index, history in undo log
  [A | 1500]  --roll-pointer-->  undo: [A | 2000] --> older...
  a snapshot reader reconstructs the old version by walking undo records.
```

Consequences worth saying out loud. Postgres UPDATE writes a whole new row version even if one column changed - hence bloat, autovacuum tuning, and the "why is my table 3x its data size" incident. InnoDB keeps the table compact but long-running transactions pin undo history and slow purge. For SERIALIZABLE they diverge fully: InnoDB falls back to locking reads with next-key locks (readers block writers again); Postgres uses SSI - Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which lets everything run optimistically, watches for dangerous read-write dependency patterns, and ABORTS one transaction instead of blocking - so Postgres serializable code must catch serialization failures and retry.

Optimistic vs pessimistic in one line each, since the interviewer will map this to app code: pessimistic = take the lock before touching (FOR UPDATE) - right when conflicts are common; optimistic = touch freely, detect conflict at write time (version column, or SSI) and retry - right when conflicts are rare, because retries are cheaper than everyone queueing.
sections.code:
# Postgres-style MVCC visibility, executable. Row versions carry xmin/xmax;
# a snapshot sees a version iff creator committed before it and any deleter did not.
def visible(version, snapshot_xid, committed):
    created_ok = version["xmin"] in committed and version["xmin"] < snapshot_xid
    deleted    = (version["xmax"] is not None
                  and version["xmax"] in committed and version["xmax"] < snapshot_xid)
    return created_ok and not deleted

# txn 900 updates A: 2000 -> 1500 (old version gets xmax=900; new gets xmin=900)
versions = [
    {"row": "A", "xmin": 612, "xmax": 900, "bal": 2000},
    {"row": "A", "xmin": 900, "xmax": None, "bal": 1500},
]

committed = {612}                       # txn 900 still in flight
old_reader = [v["bal"] for v in versions if visible(v, 850, committed)]
assert old_reader == [2000]             # snapshot before 900: sees old version only

committed = {612, 900}                  # 900 commits
late_reader = [v["bal"] for v in versions if visible(v, 950, committed)]
assert late_reader == [1500]            # new snapshot: sees exactly the new version

dead = [v for v in versions
        if v["xmax"] in committed and v["xmax"] is not None]
assert len(dead) == 1                   # the 2000-version is now garbage -> VACUUM's job
print("reader during update saw:", old_reader, "| after commit:", late_reader)

sections.title: 10. Query Processing and EXPLAIN
sections.content:
Why learn the pipeline: "the query is slow" is the most common database ticket you will ever get, and EXPLAIN is the only honest witness. A statement passes through four stages: the parser (text to syntax tree), the rewriter (expand views, apply rules), the planner/optimizer (choose HOW - which index, which join order, which algorithm - by estimating cost from statistics: row counts, distinct values, value histograms that ANALYZE maintains), and the executor (run the chosen plan). The optimizer is cost-based guessing, and when its row estimates are wrong, it picks wrong plans - that single sentence explains most slow-query mysteries.

The building blocks the plan is made of. Access paths: Seq Scan (read the whole table - correct choice for unselective filters), Index Scan (descend the B+ tree per match, fetch rows), Index Only Scan (covering index, section 5), and Postgres's Bitmap Scan (collect matching row addresses from the index, sort, fetch in physical order - the middle ground when matches are many). Join algorithms: Nested Loop (for each outer row, probe the inner side - excellent when the outer side is small and the inner probe hits an index), Hash Join (build a hash table on the smaller side, probe with the larger - the workhorse for big equijoins), Merge Join (both inputs sorted on the key, zip through - shines when indexes already provide the order).

Reading a real plan for "orders of customer 42 with customer name":

```
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT o.order_id, c.name FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id = 42;

Nested Loop  (cost=0.86..24.91 rows=3 width=40)
             (actual time=0.04..0.09 rows=31 loops=1)
  -> Index Scan using idx_orders_customer on orders o
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
        (actual rows=31)
  -> Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)   (actual rows=1 loops=31)
```

How to read it: inner nodes feed outer ones; "cost" is the planner's estimate (startup..total, in abstract units), "actual" is the truth EXPLAIN ANALYZE measured by really running the query. The debugging method, in order: (1) compare estimated rows vs actual rows - here 3 vs 31; a 10x gap means stale statistics, run ANALYZE, because every choice downstream of a bad estimate is suspect. (2) Look for a Seq Scan on a big table under a selective filter - "Rows Removed by Filter: 9,970,000" screams missing index. (3) Check Index Cond vs Filter: a condition listed as Filter is applied AFTER fetching rows the index could not exclude - often a composite-index column-order problem or a function wrapped around the column. (4) Only then consider rewriting the query. When an interviewer says "this query is slow, what do you do," they are testing for a METHOD - EXPLAIN ANALYZE first, estimates vs actuals, statistics, indexes - not for the word "add an index."

sections.title: 11. Recovery: WAL and Checkpoints
sections.content:
The problem: durability says a committed transfer survives a power cut, but data pages live scattered across the disk, and flushing every touched page at every commit would mean a storm of random writes - plus a crash mid-flush could leave a page half-written (a torn page). Every serious engine solves this the same way: write-ahead logging.

WAL (write-ahead log): an append-only file of change records ("txn 900: page 512, row 3, bal 2000 -> 1500"). The rule that gives it its name: the log record must reach disk BEFORE the data page it describes, and before COMMIT returns. So commit costs one sequential append + fsync (a forced flush to physical disk) - sequential I/O, the cheapest kind - while the modified data pages stay dirty (changed only in memory, in the buffer pool - the cache of disk pages) and get written back lazily, batched, whenever convenient. The log is the truth; the data files are a lagging materialization of it.

```
timeline (LSN = log sequence number, the log's byte offset):

 ...--[CHECKPOINT]--[T1: A 2000->1500]--[T1 COMMIT]--[T2: B 100->x]--CRASH
                                                        (T2 never committed)
recovery on restart:
  1. find last checkpoint record
  2. REDO forward from there: reapply every logged change
     (data pages may be stale - the log knows better)
  3. UNDO losers: T2 has no COMMIT record -> reverse its changes
result: T1's transfer survives (durability), T2 vanishes (atomicity)
```

A checkpoint is the housekeeping that keeps recovery fast: flush all dirty pages to disk and write a checkpoint record saying "everything before this LSN is safely in the data files." Without checkpoints, recovery would replay the log from the beginning of time; with them, replay starts at the last checkpoint - which is why checkpoint frequency is a knob trading runtime I/O (frequent flushing) against restart time (long replay). Postgres calls the same idea checkpoints against pg_wal; InnoDB calls its log the redo log and keeps undo separate (the undo log, which section 9 showed doing double duty for MVCC).

Two payoffs to mention that mark real understanding. First, the WAL is why COMMIT is fast: the customer waits for one sequential fsync, not for scattered page writes. Second, the WAL is bigger than recovery - it is the replication feed. Postgres streaming replication ships WAL records to replicas that replay them continuously; point-in-time recovery restores a base backup and replays archived WAL up to "right before the bad deploy at 14:02." When an interviewer asks "how does a database not lose data," the expected shape is: log record fsynced before commit returns; redo from checkpoint plus undo of uncommitted work on restart; checkpoints bound the replay.

sections.title: 12. CAP, NoSQL Families, and When Relational Still Wins
sections.content:
Once data outgrows one machine or one region, you distribute it - and the CAP theorem states the resulting bargain. Popular retellings say "pick 2 of 3: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance," which is wrong enough to fail you in an interview. The real statement: when a network partition happens (nodes alive but unable to talk - and in a distributed system this WILL happen, so P is not a choice), each side must either refuse/delay answers to stay consistent (CP) or keep answering with possibly stale data (AP). During normal, partition-free operation you can have both C and A; CAP is about behavior DURING the partition. Concrete: two datacenters split; a CP store rejects writes on the minority side (a bank blocks a withdrawal rather than risk double-spending); an AP store accepts writes on both sides and reconciles later (a shopping cart would rather show a slightly stale cart than an error page).

The NoSQL families, each defined by its query shape, with the trade named:

```
family       | examples          | model               | you give up
-------------+-------------------+---------------------+------------------------
key-value    | Redis, DynamoDB   | get/put by key      | queries on values, joins
document     | MongoDB           | JSON per aggregate  | cross-document txns/joins
                                                         (are limited/costly)
wide-column  | Cassandra         | partition -> sorted | ad-hoc queries: you model
             |                   | rows, write-tuned   | tables per query pattern
graph        | Neo4j             | nodes + edges       | throughput on non-graph work
```

BASE is the philosophy label for the AP end - Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent (replicas converge if writes stop) - the deliberate opposite of ACID's strict promises. The trade in one line: ACID makes the DATABASE keep the invariants; BASE makes YOUR APPLICATION handle stale reads, conflicting writes, and reconciliation.

When is relational still right? More often than the hype says, and interviewers increasingly test for this judgment. Choose Postgres/MySQL when you need transactions across entities (order + payment + inventory must move together), when query patterns are not known upfront (SQL joins answer questions the schema never anticipated; a wide-column store needs the query known at design time), when constraints must hold (foreign keys, uniqueness - in BASE systems these become application code and on-call pages), and when scale actually fits - a single well-indexed Postgres comfortably serves hundreds of gigabytes and tens of thousands of QPS, which covers most products that will ever exist. Reach for NoSQL on a NAMED reason: key-value cache for session lookups at microsecond latency; Cassandra for append-heavy time-series across regions; document store when each record is a self-contained aggregate fetched whole. The strong closing line in an interview: "default to relational for correctness and query flexibility; move a specific workload out when I can name the access pattern and the consistency I am giving up."

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
interviewQA.a: Both enforce uniqueness, so start with what differs. A table can carry many unique constraints but exactly one primary key - the PK is the elected candidate key that gives rows their identity, and foreign keys in other tables point at it. PK columns are implicitly NOT NULL; a unique column may hold NULL, and in Postgres and MySQL several NULLs pass the same unique constraint because NULL compares as unknown. Then add the physical layer, which is what the interviewer is really probing: in InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index - the table's rows physically live in the PK's B+ tree, and every secondary index stores a copy of the PK in its leaves, so a wide PK (say a UUID string) inflates every index on the table. A unique key is an ordinary secondary index with a uniqueness check. Concrete example: customers has candidate keys customer_id and email; pick customer_id as PK because it is compact and never changes, keep email UNIQUE as an alternate key.
followUps: Why prefer an integer surrogate key over a natural key like email?
What happens to secondary index size in InnoDB if the PK is a 36-char UUID?
Can a foreign key reference a unique key instead of a primary key?

interviewQA.q: Explain normalization. How far do you actually normalize in production?
interviewQA.a: Normalization removes redundancy so every fact lives in one place, because duplicated facts drift apart. I explain it with anomalies: if orders repeat the customer's city, updating her city must touch many rows (update anomaly), a customer without orders cannot exist (insert anomaly), and deleting her last order erases her (delete anomaly). The forms, via 'the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key': 1NF - atomic values, no lists in a cell; 2NF - no column depending on part of a composite key (item_name depends on item_id alone, not on (order_id, item_id), so it moves to menu_items); 3NF - no transitive dependencies (order -> customer_id -> city means city moves to customers); BCNF - every determinant is a candidate key, which catches corner cases like a courier determining a zone. In production I design to 3NF/BCNF by default, then denormalize specific measured hot paths - e.g., store orders.total_amount instead of summing order_items on every page load - accepting that every write must now maintain the copy and that a bug can make the copy disagree with the truth.
followUps: Give a table that is in 3NF but not BCNF.
Is storing price_at_order in order_items denormalization? Why not?
What breaks first when a denormalized copy goes out of sync, and how would you detect it?

interviewQA.q: How does a B+ tree index work internally, and why not a hash table or binary search tree?
interviewQA.a: A B+ tree is a balanced tree built from disk pages: internal nodes hold only separator keys for routing, all real entries sit in the leaves, and leaves are linked left-to-right. Because a node is a 16KB page, fanout is in the hundreds - with fanout 300, three levels index 27 million keys, so any point lookup is about 3 page reads, and the top levels stay cached. That answers 'why not a binary search tree': fanout 2 would need 25 levels, meaning 25 disk reads. Against a hash index: hashing gives O(1) exact-match lookups but destroys order, so range predicates (placed_at > yesterday), prefix matches, and ORDER BY get nothing from it - while a B+ tree serves a range with one descent plus a walk along the linked leaves. The interviewer is testing whether you connect the structure to disk I/O: the design goal is minimizing page reads, and everything about the B+ tree (page-sized nodes, high fanout, linked leaves) follows from that.
followUps: What happens inside the tree when a leaf page fills up on INSERT?
Why are B+ tree leaves linked to each other - which query shape uses that?
When would a hash index actually be the better choice?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
interviewQA.a: A clustered index IS the table: the full rows live in the leaf pages of that index, so the table is physically ordered by its key and there is at most one per table. In InnoDB the primary key is always the clustered index. A non-clustered (secondary) index is a separate B+ tree whose leaves hold the indexed columns plus a pointer to the row - in InnoDB that pointer is the primary key value, so a secondary-index lookup costs two tree descents: secondary tree to find the PK, then the clustered tree to find the row. Consequences worth naming: PK range scans are fast in InnoDB because neighbors on disk are neighbors by key; a fat PK bloats every secondary index because each leaf carries a copy of it. Postgres is the contrast that shows real understanding: tables are unordered heaps, every index is secondary, and leaves store a TID (physical row address) - so there is no two-descent pattern, one descent plus a heap fetch, and no index dictates row order.
followUps: Why does InnoDB use the PK as the row pointer in secondary indexes instead of a physical address?
What does Postgres's CLUSTER command do, and why does the effect decay?
How does a covering index eliminate the second lookup?

interviewQA.q: Why not add an index on every column?
interviewQA.a: Because indexes are not free at write time, at planning time, or in storage. Every INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column, or DELETE must modify every index - a table with 5 secondary indexes turns one logical row write into 6 B+ tree modifications, plus more WAL, so write throughput drops as indexes accumulate. Second, selectivity: an index on orders.status with 3 values matches roughly a third of a 10M-row table; fetching 3M rows through random index hops is slower than one sequential scan, so the optimizer ignores the index and you paid its write cost for nothing. Third, unused indexes still consume disk and buffer-pool memory, evicting pages that useful indexes needed, and they widen the planner's search space. The habit to describe: index what the query patterns need - columns in WHERE with high selectivity, join keys, ORDER BY prefixes - verify usage with EXPLAIN, and drop indexes that pg_stat_user_indexes or sys.schema_unused_indexes show as never scanned.
followUps: How would you find unused indexes in a running Postgres or MySQL instance?
Why might the optimizer skip an index even when the column appears in WHERE?
What is write amplification, and how do LSM-based stores change this trade?

interviewQA.q: Explain the four isolation levels and what anomaly each one eliminates.
interviewQA.a: I draw the table: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms; READ COMMITTED removes dirty reads (each statement sees only committed data as of that statement's start); REPEATABLE READ removes non-repeatable reads (the whole transaction reads one snapshot, so a re-read row cannot change); SERIALIZABLE removes phantoms and everything else - the outcome must equal some serial ordering. Then the engine notes that show depth: Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED, and its READ UNCOMMITTED silently behaves as READ COMMITTED because MVCC never exposes uncommitted versions. Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation - it also prevents phantoms, but permits write skew, which is why its SERIALIZABLE (SSI) exists and answers with serialization-failure aborts you must retry. InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ and uses next-key locks on locking reads to block phantom inserts. Choosing: default level plus SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for read-modify-write, SERIALIZABLE when an invariant spans rows and retries are acceptable.
followUps: What is write skew, and why does snapshot isolation not prevent it?
Why does Postgres READ UNCOMMITTED behave like READ COMMITTED?
What does your application code need to handle when running SERIALIZABLE in Postgres?

interviewQA.q: Show me a dirty read, a non-repeatable read, and a phantom - with actual interleavings.
interviewQA.a: Dirty read - T1: BEGIN, UPDATE accounts SET bal=1500 WHERE id='A'. T2: SELECT bal WHERE id='A' and sees 1500 while it is uncommitted. T1: ROLLBACK. T2 acted on a value that never existed in any committed state. Non-repeatable read - T2: BEGIN, SELECT bal WHERE id='A' -> 2000. T1: UPDATE to 1500, COMMIT. T2: same SELECT again -> 1500; the same row changed inside one transaction, so a validate-then-act sequence in T2 is now acting on stale validation. Phantom - T2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE city='Pune' -> 10. T1: INSERT a new Pune order, COMMIT. T2 repeats the COUNT -> 11. The key distinction from a non-repeatable read: no row T2 previously read was modified - a NEW row entered the predicate, so locking the rows you read cannot prevent it; you need gap/predicate locking (InnoDB next-key locks) or a fixed snapshot (Postgres REPEATABLE READ). I would also volunteer the lost update - two read-modify-writes overwriting each other - since it is the anomaly that actually costs money in application code.
followUps: Why can't row locks alone prevent phantoms?
Which of these anomalies can occur at READ COMMITTED in Postgres?
Write the interleaving for a lost update and give two different fixes.

interviewQA.q: ACID vs BASE - what does each promise, and when is each the right trade?
interviewQA.a: ACID is the single-database contract: Atomicity (a bank transfer's debit and credit both happen or neither does - undo logs make half-done work reversible), Consistency (each transaction moves the database between valid states - constraints plus application invariants), Isolation (concurrent transactions cannot see each other's intermediate states - an auditor never sees the money mid-flight), Durability (once COMMIT returns, a power cut loses nothing - the WAL record is fsynced first). BASE - Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent - is the distributed-availability philosophy: keep answering during failures and partitions, accept stale reads, let replicas converge later. The real content of the question is who owns correctness: under ACID the database enforces invariants; under BASE your application must tolerate stale data, resolve conflicting writes, and reconcile. Pick ACID where an invariant must never be observed broken - money, inventory, bookings. Pick BASE where availability beats freshness - shopping carts, feeds, view counters - and say the criterion out loud: what is the cost of a stale read versus the cost of refusing service?
followUps: Where does 'eventually consistent' actually show up as a bug in application code?
Can you get ACID transactions in a distributed SQL database - what does it cost?
Map BASE to the AP side of CAP: what happens during a partition?

interviewQA.q: How does MVCC work in Postgres, and do readers block writers?
interviewQA.a: MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row so that readers never block writers and writers never block readers - that is the headline, and then I explain the mechanics. Every Postgres row version carries xmin (the transaction id that created it) and xmax (the one that deleted or superseded it). An UPDATE does not modify in place: it appends a new version with xmin = my txn id and stamps the old version's xmax. Every transaction (or statement, at READ COMMITTED) gets a snapshot, and a version is visible if its creator committed before the snapshot and its deleter had not - so a reader concurrent with an in-flight update sees the old version, no waiting. Writers do block each other: two UPDATEs on one row serialize on a row-level exclusive lock. The operational tail is what distinguishes a strong answer: superseded versions are dead but occupy heap pages - bloat - and VACUUM/autovacuum reclaims them; long-running transactions hold old snapshots and prevent cleanup. InnoDB reaches the same behavior differently: one current row in the clustered index, old versions reconstructed from the undo log.
followUps: Why do long-running transactions cause bloat in Postgres?
How does InnoDB reconstruct an old row version for a snapshot reader?
If readers never block, why do two concurrent UPDATEs to the same row still queue?

interviewQA.q: What is a deadlock in a database, and what does the engine do about it?
interviewQA.a: A deadlock is a cycle of transactions each holding a lock the next one needs: T1 locks row A (say account 1) and then requests row B; T2 already locks B and requests A; both wait forever. Engines handle it by detection, not prevention: InnoDB maintains a waits-for graph and checks for cycles when a lock wait begins; Postgres checks after deadlock_timeout (default 1s). On detection the engine picks a victim - typically the transaction that did the least work - and aborts it with a deadlock error; the other proceeds. Two things the interviewer wants beyond the definition. First, the application response: a deadlock error is not a bug in the database, it is a retryable condition - wrap the transaction in a retry loop. Second, prevention in your own code: acquire locks in a globally consistent order (always update the lower account id first, so the A-B / B-A pattern cannot form), keep transactions short, and avoid user interaction between BEGIN and COMMIT so locks are held for milliseconds, not minutes.
followUps: How does lock ordering prevent the cycle - walk through the transfer example.
What is lock escalation, and why does InnoDB's row locking make deadlocks more or less likely than table locks?
How is a deadlock different from a lock wait timeout, and how does your code tell them apart?

interviewQA.q: A production query is slow. Walk me through how you would debug it.
interviewQA.a: Method, not guesses. First reproduce with EXPLAIN ANALYZE (it runs the query and prints the real plan with actual times and row counts; plain EXPLAIN shows only estimates). Second, compare estimated rows vs actual rows at each node: a 10x-100x gap means the planner chose the plan on wrong statistics - run ANALYZE to refresh them and re-check, because every downstream choice (join order, algorithm) was based on the bad estimate. Third, look for the classic shapes: a Seq Scan on a large table with 'Rows Removed by Filter' in the millions under a selective predicate means a missing index; a condition appearing as Filter instead of Index Cond means the index cannot serve it - usually a function wrapped around the column (lower(email)) or wrong column order in a composite index; a Nested Loop whose inner side is a Seq Scan executed thousands of times means a missing index on the join key. Fourth, check whether a covering index could make it index-only. Only after the plan is sane do I consider rewriting the query or caching. This ordering matters: measure, fix statistics, fix access paths, then restructure.
followUps: Why can EXPLAIN ANALYZE be dangerous to run casually, and what is the safe variant for writes?
The planner estimates 3 rows, actual is 300,000. Name two causes and their fixes.
The query was fast yesterday and slow today with no code change - what are your first three hypotheses?

interviewQA.q: What is write-ahead logging, and why write the log before the data?
interviewQA.a: WAL solves two problems at once: durability without random I/O, and atomicity across crashes. Every change is first appended as a record to a sequential log file, and the rule that names the technique is: the log record must be fsynced to disk before the data page it describes is written, and before COMMIT returns to the client. That makes commit cost one sequential append + fsync - cheap - while the actual data pages stay dirty in the buffer pool and are flushed lazily in batches. If the machine dies, the log is the truth: recovery replays it forward from the last checkpoint (redo), reapplying changes the data files never received, then reverses changes of transactions that lack a COMMIT record (undo) - which is exactly how a half-done bank transfer disappears instead of leaving money missing. Reversing the order would break the guarantee: if the data page reached disk before its log record and the crash hit between, you would have a change on disk that recovery knows nothing about and cannot undo. Checkpoints bound the story: flush dirty pages, mark the log position, and recovery replays from there rather than from the beginning of time. Bonus: WAL shipping is also how streaming replication and point-in-time recovery work.
followUps: What exactly does a checkpoint trade off - what gets worse if checkpoints are very frequent?
How does WAL enable point-in-time recovery to 'right before the bad deploy'?
What is a torn page, and how do full-page writes in the WAL handle it?

interviewQA.q: Two requests read a wallet balance of 100 and each writes back 110. The user deposited twice but the balance shows 110. What happened and how do you fix it?
interviewQA.a: This is a lost update: two concurrent read-modify-write transactions, both read 100, both computed 100+10, and the second write overwrote the first - one deposit vanished. Note that READ COMMITTED does not stop this: both reads saw committed data. Fixes, strongest first. (1) Make the operation atomic in SQL: UPDATE wallets SET bal = bal + 10 WHERE id = 7 - the read and write become one statement under a row lock, so the second UPDATE waits and applies on top of 110. This is the right fix whenever the new value is computable in SQL. (2) Pessimistic: SELECT bal FROM wallets WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE inside the transaction - the row lock is held from the read to the commit, so the second transaction's read blocks until the first commits. Needed when application code must compute the new value. (3) Optimistic: a version column - UPDATE ... SET bal=110, version=8 WHERE id=7 AND version=7; zero rows affected means someone else won, so re-read and retry. Choose optimistic when conflicts are rare (cheap, no held locks), pessimistic when contention is high (retries would thrash).
followUps: Why doesn't REPEATABLE READ in Postgres silently fix this - what error do you get instead?
How would you implement the optimistic version check in an ORM like Hibernate or Django?
When does FOR UPDATE start hurting throughput, and what is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for?

interviewQA.q: When would you choose a NoSQL database over Postgres?
interviewQA.a: Only with a named access pattern and a named consistency sacrifice - that framing is the answer's skeleton. Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) when the workload is get/put by a known key at very high volume or sub-millisecond latency - sessions, feature flags, caches - and I give up value queries and joins. Document (MongoDB) when each record is a self-contained aggregate read and written whole, with per-record structure variation - a product catalog - and I give up cheap cross-document joins and accept limited cross-document transactions. Wide-column (Cassandra) for append-heavy, time-ordered writes at multi-region scale - metrics, events - accepting that tables are modeled per query and ad-hoc questions need new tables or Spark. Graph (Neo4j) when the queries are traversals ('friends of friends who ordered from this restaurant'). Against that: Postgres wins whenever I need transactions spanning entities, constraints enforced by the database, or query patterns I cannot predict - and one tuned instance serves hundreds of GB and tens of thousands of QPS, which covers most systems. Default relational; migrate a specific workload when it outgrows that, not the whole product.
followUps: Your product's data is 50 GB and growing 2 GB/month. Is 'we need to scale' a reason for Cassandra?
How do you keep referential integrity in a document store - who enforces it now?
What does Postgres's JSONB change about the 'flexible schema' argument for MongoDB?

interviewQA.q: State the CAP theorem precisely. What do people usually get wrong?
interviewQA.a: The wrong version is 'pick two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance,' as if P were optional. The precise version: in a distributed system, network partitions - nodes alive but unable to communicate - will happen, so P is a fact, not a choice. The theorem says that DURING a partition you must choose per operation: respond only if you can guarantee consistency (CP - the minority side refuses or delays writes; a payment system blocks rather than risk double-spending), or always respond, possibly with stale data (AP - both sides accept writes and reconcile after healing; a shopping cart prefers staleness to an error page). During normal operation there is no C/A trade at all - you can have both. Two refinements that signal depth: C in CAP means linearizability (every read sees the latest completed write), a much stronger claim than ACID's C, which is about invariants; and PACELC extends the theorem to normal operation - Else, when there is no partition, you still trade Latency against Consistency, which is why even healthy systems offer eventual-consistency read modes (DynamoDB's cheaper stale reads) for latency.
followUps: Where does a single-node Postgres sit in CAP terms - is the question even well-posed?
Explain PACELC and give a system that chooses latency over consistency with no partition.
What does 'C' mean differently in CAP versus in ACID?

interviewQA.q: Walk me through what happens inside the database between BEGIN and COMMIT for a single UPDATE.
interviewQA.a: Take UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 'A' in Postgres. BEGIN allocates transaction state; the txn id is assigned at first write. The executor finds the row via the index on id (B+ tree descent to a heap TID), and takes a row-level exclusive lock so a concurrent UPDATE of the same row waits. MVCC write: the old version is not overwritten - a new version with the new balance is written (xmin = my txn id) and the old version's xmax is stamped; concurrent readers with older snapshots continue to see the old version, unblocked. Each change is described as WAL records in memory; the touched pages become dirty in the buffer pool. COMMIT is the critical step: the commit record and preceding WAL are fsynced to disk - only after that fsync succeeds does COMMIT return, which IS the durability promise - then the transaction is marked committed, locks release, and waiters proceed. Dirty pages flush later; checkpoints bound how much WAL a crash would replay. On ROLLBACK instead: mark aborted, and the new version is never visible to anyone - VACUUM eventually reclaims it.
followUps: What changes in this story for InnoDB, where updates happen in place?
Why does COMMIT wait for the WAL fsync but not for data-page writes?
What does synchronous_commit=off change, and what do you risk?

interviewQA.q: Explain WHERE vs HAVING, and why the SQL clause order makes aliases invisible to WHERE.
interviewQA.a: The logical execution order decides everything here: FROM/JOIN, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. WHERE runs before grouping, so it filters individual rows and cannot reference aggregates - 'WHERE COUNT(*) > 10' is meaningless because no groups exist yet. HAVING runs after GROUP BY, filtering whole groups, and exists precisely so aggregate conditions have a home: HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10 keeps cities with ten delivered orders. Performance corollary: push every plain row condition into WHERE (status = 'delivered'), because discarding rows before grouping shrinks the grouping work; a row condition placed in HAVING gives the same result but groups rows it will throw away. Aliases: SELECT runs fifth, so a name it creates (COUNT(*) AS orders_cnt) does not exist when WHERE runs third - hence 'unknown column orders_cnt in WHERE' - while ORDER BY, running after SELECT, can use it. Same reasoning explains the LEFT JOIN trap: a right-side condition in WHERE runs after the join and filters out the NULL-extended rows, silently turning the outer join into an inner one; the condition belongs in ON.
followUps: Why does putting a right-table condition in WHERE break a LEFT JOIN, in clause-order terms?
Is the written order ever the physical execution order? What is the optimizer allowed to change?
Where does DISTINCT fit in the logical order, and why does it come after SELECT?

flashcards.front: Superkey vs candidate key vs primary key?
flashcards.back: Superkey: any column set that uniquely identifies a row. Candidate key: a MINIMAL superkey. Primary key: the one candidate key elected for identity; the others become alternate keys with UNIQUE constraints.

flashcards.front: Primary key vs unique constraint - three differences?
flashcards.back: One PK per table vs many uniques; PK is implicitly NOT NULL, unique columns may hold NULLs (often several); in InnoDB the PK is the clustered index that physically orders the table, a unique key is a separate secondary index.

flashcards.front: What does a foreign key enforce, and what are the ON DELETE options?
flashcards.back: Referential integrity: the child value must exist in the parent's key (orders.customer_id must exist in customers). ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks the parent delete, CASCADE deletes children, SET NULL orphans them explicitly.

flashcards.front: How is an M:N relationship stored in a relational database?
flashcards.back: A junction table whose composite PK is the two foreign keys, e.g. order_items(order_id, item_id). Attributes of the relationship itself (qty, price_at_order) live on the junction table, not on either entity.

flashcards.front: Where does the foreign key go in a 1:N relationship?
flashcards.back: On the N side. A customer has many orders, so orders carries customer_id. The 1 side cannot hold it: one column stores one value, not a list of ids.

flashcards.front: What is a weak entity and how is it mapped to a table?
flashcards.back: An entity with no identity of its own (menu item numbered per restaurant). Its table's PK is composite: the owner's key plus a local discriminator, e.g. PRIMARY KEY (restaurant_id, item_number).

flashcards.front: Name the three anomalies unnormalized data causes.
flashcards.back: Update anomaly (one fact stored in many rows drifts when edited), insert anomaly (cannot record an entity without an unrelated one, e.g. a restaurant with no orders), delete anomaly (deleting the last referencing row erases the entity).

flashcards.front: 1NF in one line?
flashcards.back: Atomic values: no lists or repeating groups inside a cell. '2x Roll, 1x Coke' in one column becomes one row per item, so SQL can filter and join on items.

flashcards.front: 2NF in one line, with the running example?
flashcards.back: No partial dependencies: no column may depend on part of a composite key. With key (order_id, item_id), item_name depends on item_id alone, so it moves out to menu_items.

flashcards.front: 3NF in one line, with the running example?
flashcards.back: No transitive dependencies: no non-key column determined by another non-key column. order_id -> customer_id -> city, so city moves to the customers table.

flashcards.front: BCNF in one line - and the classic shape that is 3NF but not BCNF?
flashcards.back: Every determinant must be a candidate key. Shape: shifts(courier_id, hour, zone) with courier_id -> zone and candidate keys {courier_id,hour} and {zone,hour}: courier_id determines zone but is not a key. Fix: split out courier_zone(courier_id, zone).

flashcards.front: When is denormalization justified?
flashcards.back: When a MEASURED hot read path is slow because of a join/aggregate (e.g. orders.total_amount instead of summing order_items per page load), writes are comparatively rare, and you accept that every write must maintain the copy.

flashcards.front: SQL logical clause execution order?
flashcards.back: FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT. Explains why WHERE cannot see SELECT aliases but ORDER BY can, and why aggregate filters need HAVING.

flashcards.front: WHERE vs HAVING?
flashcards.back: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping (cheap, cannot use aggregates); HAVING filters whole groups AFTER aggregation (COUNT(*) >= 10). Plain row conditions belong in WHERE so the group step has less work.

flashcards.front: LEFT JOIN trap: condition on the right table in WHERE vs in ON?
flashcards.back: In ON, unmatched left rows survive with NULLs. In WHERE, the condition runs after the join and NULLs fail it, silently converting the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

flashcards.front: Why do databases use B+ trees instead of binary search trees?
flashcards.back: Nodes are disk pages, so fanout is in the hundreds: fanout 300 indexes 27M keys in 3 levels = 3 page reads (top levels cached). A binary tree would need 25 levels = 25 reads. Linked leaves give cheap range scans.

flashcards.front: B+ tree vs hash index - what does each support?
flashcards.back: Hash: O(1) exact-match only. B+ tree: exact match, range predicates (>, BETWEEN), prefix match, and sorted output for ORDER BY - one descent then walk the linked leaves. That versatility is why B+ trees are the default.

flashcards.front: Clustered vs secondary index in InnoDB?
flashcards.back: Clustered = the table: full rows live in the PK's B+ tree leaves; one per table. Secondary index leaves hold indexed columns + the PK value, so a secondary lookup is two descents: secondary tree -> PK -> clustered tree -> row.

flashcards.front: What is a covering index / index-only scan?
flashcards.back: An index containing every column the query needs, so the table is never touched. (customer_id, placed_at) covers SELECT placed_at WHERE customer_id=42 ORDER BY placed_at: equality on column 1, presorted on column 2.

flashcards.front: Name four situations where an index hurts or is useless.
flashcards.back: 1) Write-heavy tables: every write updates every index. 2) Low selectivity (status with 3 values): scan wins. 3) Function on the column (lower(email)) defeats a plain index - need an expression index. 4) Tiny tables: one page, scan beats descent.

flashcards.front: ACID - each letter with its mechanism?
flashcards.back: Atomicity: all-or-nothing via undo (undo log / old versions). Consistency: valid state to valid state via constraints + app invariants. Isolation: no seeing half-done work, via locks/MVCC per isolation level. Durability: committed = survives crash, via WAL fsync before COMMIT returns.

flashcards.front: Dirty read in one interleaving?
flashcards.back: T1 updates bal to 1500, uncommitted. T2 reads 1500 and acts on it. T1 rolls back. T2 used a value that never existed in any committed state. Eliminated at READ COMMITTED and above.

flashcards.front: Non-repeatable read vs phantom - the precise difference?
flashcards.back: Non-repeatable: a row you already read changes on re-read (T1 updated it between). Phantom: no read row changed, but NEW rows enter your predicate on re-query (T1 inserted). Row locks stop the first, not the second - phantoms need gap locks or snapshots.

flashcards.front: Lost update: what is it and what are the three fixes?
flashcards.back: Two read-modify-writes both read 100, both write 110 - one lost. Fixes: atomic UPDATE (bal = bal + 10); pessimistic SELECT ... FOR UPDATE holding the row lock from read to commit; optimistic version column with retry when 0 rows match.

flashcards.front: Isolation levels table: which anomalies survive at each level?
flashcards.back: READ UNCOMMITTED: dirty + non-repeatable + phantom. READ COMMITTED: non-repeatable + phantom. REPEATABLE READ: phantom (per the standard; Postgres snapshot RR blocks phantoms too but allows write skew). SERIALIZABLE: none.

flashcards.front: Default isolation level of Postgres and of MySQL/InnoDB?
flashcards.back: Postgres: READ COMMITTED (its READ UNCOMMITTED behaves identically - MVCC never shows uncommitted data). InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ, with next-key locks on locking reads to block phantom inserts.

flashcards.front: What is write skew, and which level stops it?
flashcards.back: Two txns read overlapping data, each writes a DIFFERENT row, and the combination breaks an invariant (both on-call doctors remove themselves). Snapshot isolation allows it; SERIALIZABLE (Postgres SSI) detects and aborts one txn - code must retry.

flashcards.front: MVCC in one sentence - and who still blocks whom?
flashcards.back: Keep multiple row versions and give each transaction a snapshot, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Writers still block writers: concurrent UPDATEs of the same row queue on its exclusive row lock.

flashcards.front: Postgres row versioning: xmin, xmax, and VACUUM?
flashcards.back: Each version stores xmin (creating txn) and xmax (deleting/superseding txn). UPDATE appends a new version and stamps the old one's xmax. A snapshot sees versions whose creator committed and deleter had not. Dead versions = bloat; VACUUM reclaims them.

flashcards.front: How does InnoDB provide old row versions without keeping them in the table?
flashcards.back: The clustered index holds only the current version with a roll pointer into the undo log; snapshot readers walk undo records to reconstruct the version their read view needs. Purge threads discard undo history no view can need.

flashcards.front: Deadlock: definition, engine response, and your two defenses?
flashcards.back: A cycle of transactions each waiting for a lock the next holds. Engine detects (waits-for graph or timeout) and aborts a victim. Defenses: retry the victim; acquire locks in a consistent global order (lower account id first) and keep transactions short.

flashcards.front: The WAL rule, and why commit is fast because of it?
flashcards.back: Log records are fsynced to disk BEFORE the data pages they describe and before COMMIT returns. Commit = one sequential append+fsync; dirty data pages flush lazily. Crash recovery: redo the log from the last checkpoint, undo uncommitted transactions.

flashcards.front: What does a checkpoint do and what does its frequency trade?
flashcards.back: Flushes all dirty pages and records 'everything before this log position is in the data files', so recovery replays only from there. Frequent checkpoints: more runtime I/O, fast restart. Rare: cheap runtime, long crash recovery.

flashcards.front: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and the first thing to compare in the output?
flashcards.back: EXPLAIN prints the planner's estimated plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and adds actual times and row counts. First check: estimated rows vs actual rows per node - a large gap means stale statistics (run ANALYZE) and an untrustworthy plan.

flashcards.front: The three join algorithms and when each wins?
flashcards.back: Nested loop: small outer side + index on inner join key. Hash join: large equijoins - build a hash on the smaller input, probe with the larger. Merge join: both inputs already sorted on the key (e.g. via indexes), zip through them.

flashcards.front: CAP theorem, stated correctly?
flashcards.back: Partitions will happen (P is not optional). DURING a partition, choose per operation: consistency (refuse/delay - CP) or availability (answer possibly stale - AP). With no partition you can have both; PACELC adds the latency/consistency trade of normal operation.

flashcards.front: The four NoSQL families with one example and one sacrifice each?
flashcards.back: Key-value (Redis/DynamoDB): no value queries or joins. Document (MongoDB): weak cross-document joins/transactions. Wide-column (Cassandra): query-first modeling, no ad-hoc queries. Graph (Neo4j): specialized for traversals, not general throughput.

flashcards.front: When is a relational database still the right default?
flashcards.back: Transactions spanning entities (order+payment+inventory), unpredictable/ad-hoc query patterns needing joins, database-enforced constraints, and scale that fits one machine - a tuned Postgres serves hundreds of GB and tens of thousands of QPS.
